terms.Trunk-based development: Trunk-based development (TBD) means developers integrate into one shared branch at least daily, either by committing directly or through very short-lived branches and pull requests that merge within hours. Its prerequisites are fast, reliable CI, a strong automated test suite, fast reviews and feature flags that decouple deployment from release. The DORA research associates it with higher delivery performance, because integration cost grows with branch age and divergence. Release branches may still be cut for hotfixes, but fixes land on trunk first and are cherry-picked out. Contrast it with GitFlow, whose long-lived develop and release branches suit versioned products with several supported versions but slow down continuous deployment.
terms.Reflog: The reflog is a per-repository, per-ref log stored under .git/logs that records each old and new SHA whenever HEAD or a branch moves, through commit, reset, rebase, checkout, merge or amend. Syntax such as HEAD@{3} or main@{yesterday} addresses entries. Reachable entries expire after 90 days by default and unreachable ones after 30 (gc.reflogExpire and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable); after that git gc can prune the objects. It is purely local: clones and remotes have their own. ORIG_HEAD offers a one-step undo after reset, merge or rebase, and git fsck --lost-found finds dangling commits that no reflog entry references.
terms.Container: Technically, a container is a process tree started with its own Linux namespaces (PID, mount, network, UTS, IPC, user), constrained by cgroups for CPU, memory and I/O, and hardened with seccomp, dropped capabilities and LSMs such as AppArmor or SELinux. Its root filesystem is an overlay of read-only image layers plus a writable layer. The OCI runtime spec standardizes how runtimes like runc create it, and containerd or CRI-O manage its lifecycle. Because the kernel is shared, isolation is weaker than with hardware virtualization; sandboxes such as gVisor, Kata Containers or Firecracker microVMs trade a little overhead for stronger multi-tenant boundaries.
terms.Container image: An OCI image consists of a manifest that references a JSON config (entrypoint, env, user, working directory, history) and an ordered list of compressed tar layers, each identified by a SHA-256 digest. Content addressing enables deduplication: identical base layers are stored and pulled once. An image index groups per-platform manifests for multi-architecture images. Tags are mutable names; digests are immutable, so production deploys should pin digests. Deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it from earlier ones, which is how secrets leak. Supply-chain metadata such as signatures (cosign), SBOMs and provenance attestations can be attached alongside an image in the registry.
terms.Dockerfile: A Dockerfile is processed by BuildKit, which builds a dependency graph of instructions, runs independent stages in parallel and caches each step by the previous layer plus instruction text, or file checksums for COPY and ADD. Only RUN, COPY and ADD add filesystem layers; ENV, LABEL, EXPOSE and CMD change metadata. Prefer exec-form CMD and ENTRYPOINT so the app is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM, use ARG for build-time values and ENV for runtime ones, and add a non-root USER. BuildKit extensions such as RUN --mount=type=cache and --mount=type=secret speed builds and keep credentials out of layers. A .dockerignore keeps the build context small and the cache stable.
terms.Multi-stage build: Each FROM in a Dockerfile begins a stage that can be named with AS. Only the final stage, or the one selected with --target, becomes the output image, and COPY --from=<stage> copies chosen artifacts from earlier stages or even from other images. BuildKit skips stages the target does not depend on. Typical results: a Go service shrinks from roughly 900 MB to 10-20 MB on scratch or distroless static, though scratch lacks CA certificates, time zone data and a shell. Targets also enable one Dockerfile with test, dev and prod stages. Smaller images mean faster pulls, quicker autoscaling and fewer packages for vulnerability scanners to flag.
terms.Docker Compose: Compose implements the Compose Specification; v2 ships as a Docker CLI plugin (docker compose), and the top-level version key is obsolete. It names resources with a project prefix, creates a default network with DNS-based service discovery, and recreates only services whose configuration changed. Key features: override files merged in order, profiles for optional services, variable interpolation from .env with ${VAR:-default}, secrets mounted under /run/secrets, depends_on conditions (service_healthy, service_completed_successfully) and Compose Watch for live sync. docker compose config prints the merged result. It lacks multi-node scheduling and rolling updates, so production clusters usually move to Kubernetes.
terms.Kubernetes: Kubernetes is a declarative control system: the API server validates and stores objects in etcd (a Raft-replicated key-value store), and controllers run level-triggered reconcile loops that move actual state toward each object's spec and report status. The scheduler binds Pods to nodes; kubelets run them through the CRI; CNI plugins provide a flat Pod network; kube-proxy or eBPF implements Services. It is extensible through CustomResourceDefinitions, admission webhooks and operators. Minor releases arrive about every four months with roughly a year of support. Managed offerings such as EKS, GKE and AKS run the control plane, but teams still own upgrades, security and capacity.
terms.Pod: A Pod's containers share a network namespace (one IP, a shared port space, localhost), IPC, and optionally volumes and a process namespace. The pause container holds the namespaces. Init containers run to completion first; native sidecars are init containers with restartPolicy: Always and run for the Pod's life. Pods are immutable in most fields and never rescheduled: a controller replaces them. Key spec fields include resources, probes, securityContext, serviceAccountName, affinity, tolerations and terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 seconds). Phases are Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown, while container states such as CrashLoopBackOff appear in the status.
terms.Kubernetes Deployment: A Deployment owns ReplicaSets through ownerReferences, and each ReplicaSet owns Pods matched by an immutable label selector. Every Pod template change creates a new ReplicaSet identified by a pod-template-hash, and the controller scales new up and old down according to the strategy: RollingUpdate with maxSurge and maxUnavailable (both 25% by default) or Recreate. Old ReplicaSets are kept up to revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) for kubectl rollout undo. progressDeadlineSeconds flags stuck rollouts. Deployments suit stateless apps; StatefulSets add stable identities and per-Pod volumes, DaemonSets run one Pod per node, and Jobs run to completion.
terms.Kubernetes Service: A Service defines a label selector and ports. The EndpointSlice controller tracks the IPs of ready matching Pods, and kube-proxy (iptables, IPVS or nftables) or an eBPF dataplane load-balances the virtual ClusterIP to them. CoreDNS publishes name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Types build on each other: ClusterIP, then NodePort (30000-32767), then LoadBalancer through the cloud controller. Headless Services (clusterIP: None) return Pod IPs directly for StatefulSets, and ExternalName is a DNS CNAME. externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves client source IPs. HTTP routing by host and path is layered on top with Ingress or the Gateway API rather than one LoadBalancer per app.
terms.Health probe: Kubernetes supports httpGet, tcpSocket, exec and grpc probes tuned by initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds (default 10), timeoutSeconds (1), failureThreshold (3) and successThreshold. A startup probe blocks the other two until it passes. Readiness gates EndpointSlice membership and rollout progress; liveness triggers a container restart by the kubelet. Best practice: readiness may check critical dependencies, but liveness should only detect a wedged process, because a dependency check in liveness turns a database blip into a cluster-wide restart storm. During shutdown, failing readiness and a short preStop delay let load balancers drain. Docker HEALTHCHECK and Compose healthcheck are the single-host equivalents.
terms.Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: The HPA controller (autoscaling/v2) evaluates metrics every 15 seconds and computes desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentValue / targetValue), ignoring changes within a 10% tolerance and applying a 5-minute scale-down stabilization window by default. Resource utilization is relative to requests, so Pods without requests cannot be scaled on percentage. Metric sources include Resource (metrics-server), Pods and Object custom metrics through an adapter, and External metrics such as queue depth; KEDA extends this to event-driven scaling and scale to zero. New Pods stay Pending if nodes are full, so pair it with Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter, and avoid driving HPA and VPA from the same metric.
